subject: Vocabulary
topic: Collocations — Common Verb-Noun and Adjective-Noun Pairs (W11 B1)

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: 'She _______ a decision to resign from her job.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'MAKE a decision' is the correct collocation in English. We say: make a decision, make a mistake, make progress, make an effort. Trap: 'Do' collocates with: do homework, do business, do damage — not 'decision'; 'Take' collocates with: take action, take a break, take a risk — 'take a decision' is common in British English but 'make a decision' is the standard universal form and the expected answer in SSC exams; 'Have' does not collocate with 'decision' meaningfully.

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: 'The medicine had a _______ effect on the patient.'
questions.explanation: D is correct. 'MARKED effect' = a clearly noticeable/significant effect. This is the standard collocation used in medical and formal contexts. Trap: 'Profound effect' is also used but with more abstract/intellectual subjects ('had a profound effect on his thinking'); 'Strong effect' is possible but less idiomatic than 'marked'; 'Deep effect' is not a standard collocation in formal English. In formal prose, 'marked' = distinctly noticeable (examiner's favourite).

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: 'The company _______ a loss of ₹5 crore in the last quarter.'
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'SUFFER a loss' is the standard collocation in business and financial contexts. Similarly: suffer a defeat, suffer an injury, suffer consequences. Trap: 'Made a loss' — we 'make a profit' but not typically 'make a loss' (British English occasionally says 'make a loss' but standard usage favours 'incur' or 'suffer'); 'Did a loss' is completely wrong; 'Had a loss' is informal and not standard. SSC exams test 'suffer a loss' as the correct form.

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: 'The politician _______ a speech at the rally.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'DELIVER a speech' is the correct formal collocation. Also valid: 'give a speech' and 'make a speech'. However, 'deliver' is the most formal and is frequently expected in SSC English. Trap: 'Told a speech' — we 'tell a story/joke' but not a 'speech'; 'Said a speech' — we 'say words' but not 'say a speech'; 'Made a speech' is also correct in informal contexts but 'delivered' is the preferred formal collocation.

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: 'She _______ great importance to punctuality.'
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'ATTACH importance to something' = to regard something as important. This is a fixed idiomatic collocation in formal English. Trap: 'Give importance to' is common in informal and Indian English but not the standard idiom; 'Put importance on' is non-standard; 'Hold importance' is also non-standard. The examiner tests this distinction: in standard British English, the correct form is 'attach importance/significance to'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: 'He _______ his promise and returned the money.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'KEEP a promise' = to do what one has promised. 'Kept his promise' is the natural English collocation. Trap: 'Fulfilled his promise' is also acceptable and means completing the terms of a promise, but 'kept' is the more natural everyday collocation tested in SSC; 'Did a promise' is wrong; 'Maintained a promise' is not standard. Antonym: 'BREAK a promise' (not 'un-keep').

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: 'The earthquake _______ widespread damage across the region.'
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'CAUSE damage' is the standard collocation with natural disasters. Other strong collocations: cause harm, cause problems, cause disruption. Trap: 'Do damage' is also a valid collocation ('did a lot of damage'), but 'cause damage' is more formal and standard; 'Make damage' is incorrect; 'Take damage' — in gaming/action contexts but not standard English for natural phenomena. When in doubt between 'do' and 'cause' in SSC, 'cause' is more formal and almost always right for disasters.

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: 'The minister _______ an inquiry into the corruption allegations.'
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'ORDER an inquiry' = to officially instruct that an investigation be carried out. This is the precise formal collocation used in legal and political contexts. Trap: 'Started an inquiry' is grammatically possible but not the formal bureaucratic/legal collocation; 'Initiated an inquiry' is also acceptable and used in formal writing — however, 'ordered' specifically implies authority/command which fits 'minister'; 'Created an inquiry' is not standard.

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: 'The director _______ a new record at the box office.'
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'BREAK a record' = to surpass a previous best performance. This is a fixed collocation — you 'break' records, not 'make' or 'create' them. After breaking, you 'set a new record' or 'hold a record'. Collocations: break a record / set a record / hold a record / break into / break down / break up. Trap: 'Made a record' = to produce a music recording (different meaning); 'Did a record' = wrong; 'Created a record' = grammatically wrong in this context.

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: 'The new policy is expected to _______ a major impact on employment rates.'
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'HAVE an impact' is the correct collocation. Impact specifically collocates with 'have': have an impact, have an effect, have a bearing. Trap: 'Cause an impact' is not standard (we say 'cause damage/harm' but not 'cause an impact'); 'Create an impact' is Indian English usage but not standard formal English; 'Do an impact' is completely wrong. Memorise: HAVE an impact/effect/influence; CAUSE damage/harm/problems; MAKE progress/effort/mistake.
